Belittle

bih-LIT-uhl · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To belittle is to make someone or something seem unimportant.

He belittled her contribution in front of the whole team.

Worked Example

The senior partner belittled the intern's report in the meeting, calling it amateurish in front of the whole team.

Deliberately making someone's work seem small and worthless in front of others is exactly what belittle describes.

How Belittle Sits Among Its Neighbors

Synonyms — open each to see how it differs

disparage

disparage: speak of something as having little value or worth

minimize: represent something as smaller or less important than it is

Antonyms

praise

praise: express admiration or approval

magnify

magnify: represent something as greater or more important

How Strong Is It? — dismiss → belittle → disparage

dismiss vs. belittle

dismiss vs. belittle: To dismiss an idea is to set it aside; to belittle someone is to actively make them or their work seem small and unimportant.

disparage vs. belittle

disparage vs. belittle: Disparage is close to belittle, though it can carry a sharper, more public edge of open contempt.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — be-

prefix — be-: thoroughly (intensifying) (English)

root — little

root — little: small in size or importance (English)

Put it together

Put it together: be- ('thoroughly') + little together mean 'to make thoroughly little' -- exactly what belittle does to someone's work or worth.

Where This Word Comes From

Where This Word Comes From: Belittle is simply be- ('thoroughly') attached to the everyday word little -- and it was coined in America by Thomas Jefferson in the 1780s. British critics sneered at the upstart word, which only helped it spread. No other English word was built from little this way, so let the story be your hook: Jefferson's critics tried to belittle 'belittle' itself.
